# What this course is {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## A course organized by data *modality*

Most visualization courses are organized by **chart type**: bar week, scatter week, pie week.

This course is organized by **what the data is**:

| Weeks | Modality |
|---|---|
| 3–4 | Tabular & time-series (the "conventional" shapes) |
| 6 | Graphs & networks |
| 7 | Text |
| 8 | Images |
| 9–10 | Maps & geographic data |
| 11–13 | **Live model output** — client–server ML |

## What makes data "complex"?

- **Structure**: relationships (networks), order (time), geometry (maps), pixels (images) — meaning that doesn't fit rows × columns
- **Scale**: more rows, columns, nodes, or pixels than the eye can hold
- **Liveness**: data that arrives from an API or a model, not a file

::: {.gw-box}
The recurring question of this course: **what does this modality's structure demand of the visualization?** A bar chart of a network throws away the network.
:::

## The end of the road (so you know where we're going)

By Week 14 you will have built a **client–server ML application**:

1. A trained model served behind a **FastAPI** endpoint
2. A **Streamlit** front-end that sends inputs and **visualizes** live predictions
3. Deployed, reproducible, and defended in class

Every week's skills feed that capstone — and your **mid-term** (multi-modality Streamlit app) is the halfway checkpoint.

# How we'll work {background-color="#2E6E8E"}

## Notebooks for exploring, apps for delivering

- **Jupyter notebooks**: where analysis happens — messy, iterative, yours
- **Streamlit apps**: where results live — interactive, shareable, for *others*

This split mirrors real data-science practice: you explore in a notebook, you ship an app. From Week 5 onward, homework increasingly means **a running app**, not a rendered document.

## Tidy data: the shape everything assumes

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import plotly.express as px
df = px.data.tips()
df.head(6)
```

One row = one observation. One column = one variable. Every library this semester — pandas, seaborn, altair, plotly — assumes it.

## A first chart, and its anatomy

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.2))
ax.scatter(df["total_bill"], df["tip"], alpha=0.6, color="#2E6E8E")
ax.set_xlabel("Total bill ($)  ← axis label: units!")
ax.set_ylabel("Tip ($)")
ax.set_title("Tips vs. total bill — a title states the relationship")
ax.annotate("each mark = one party", xy=(40, 9), fontsize=9, color="#5a6672")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Figure → axes → marks → labels → title. We name the parts now so we can argue about them all semester.

## Good vs. bad: what are we optimizing?

A visualization is **good** when the reader decodes the right conclusion, *quickly* and *accurately*.

- Not beauty (though it helps)
- Not data density (though it can)
- Not effort

::: {.gw-box}
**Discussion (3 min):** think of a chart you've seen that *looked* great and told you nothing — what failed?
:::

Setup checklist is in the Week 1 chapter of the course book; we verify everyone's environment in Block 3.

## A Streamlit app is just a script

```python
# app.py  —  run with:  streamlit run app.py
import streamlit as st
import plotly.express as px

st.title("My First App")
df = px.data.tips()
st.dataframe(df)
st.scatter_chart(df, x="total_bill", y="tip")
```

Four lines of logic → an interactive web app. (How that works — the re-run model — is Week 5's whole story. Today: just make it run.)
